doc.title: Sam Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Radio, Parker and Tristano versus his brother's swing taste
summary: He grew up on Lester Young, Parker and Tristano while his brother preferred swing; thoughts on Coltrane and generational language.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Did you get into swing from the radio or just because your brother was out there doing it?

More from the radio and then of course his was more of a Swing Era, and I grew up with I guess 15 or so, in 1945 or before, I used to hear Lester Young and Charlie Parker and things, Lennie Tristano, and I grew up more with that new influence. And then of course after it came the Coltrane, after me. So yeah, I grew up with that. So I kind of went hey this is interesting, and I kind of was interested in that.
Did you ever get with your brother and say hey, check out this bop, come on, get with it.

I think I mentioned some things like that. I think he was more, you know you get stuck in your ways a little bit. So I think he liked it but I think it was more like the swing’s the thing. If it don’t swing, you know, with the recognizable thing, the other thing was a little far out, just like certain things are far out for me. I mean I’m interested like these “Stellar Explorations,” John Coltrane you know. But I mean it’s interesting but I don’t know if I’d want to go there, or could go there.
Yeah. That’s a ways out there.
Yeah, that’s what I meant. So I mean it seems like it’s just a different twist on the language. And if you’re not in that generation, not everybody picks up the new language.
That’s a good way to put it.
That’s the way I kind of—
